clusters.canonical_name: PE Format Header Traversal as Foundational Primitive
clusters.rationale: Five convergence/coverage notes across multiple atlas batches all identify PE parsing (IMAGE_DOS_HEADER, IMAGE_NT_HEADERS, Optional Header, DataDirectory, IMAGE_EXPORT_DIRECTORY) as a cross-cutting prerequisite for SSN resolution, export hijack, module stomping, and thread hijack.
clusters.consolidated_description: A foundational reference card documenting the PE format traversal required by T-002, T-004, T-006, T-007, T-008, T-013, T-016, and T-017. Walk the IMAGE_DOS_HEADER (e_magic 0x5A4D "MZ", e_lfanew at offset 0x3C), then IMAGE_NT_HEADERS64 (Signature "PE\0\0"), IMAGE_FILE_HEADER, IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER64 (Magic 0x20B for PE32+), and DataDirectory entries. Critical offsets: IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_EXPORT (index 0) for export table traversal to resolve SSNs and function pointers; IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_BASERELOC (index 5) for relocation-aware module stomping; IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_IAT (index 12) for IAT hooking. The export table walk dereferences IMAGE_EXPORT_DIRECTORY.Name (RVAs to function names), NumberOfNames, AddressOfNames, AddressOfFunctions, AddressOfNameOrdinals — required by both SysWhispers-style SSN resolution and export-hijack DLLs. Without this card, T-002 (syscalls) and T-013 (thread hijack) become hard to navigate for readers without prior PE internals background.

clusters.canonical_name: NTDLL Unhook Method Typology and Restore Sequence
clusters.rationale: Three notes (one gap, two convergence) describe the same three-variant NTDLL unhook technique; consolidating them produces one canonical typology card rather than three fragments.
clusters.consolidated_description: Documents the three canonical NTDLL unhook variants and their concrete API sequences. (1) Byte-level prologue patch: per-function search-and-replace of the EDR's trampoline bytes with the original Nt* prologue (the inverse of the inline-hook byte forensics pattern). (2) Fresh-copy file mapping: CreateFileA(L"\\??\\C:\\Windows\\System32\\ntdll.dll") → CreateFileMapping(PAGE_READONLY | SEC_IMAGE) → MapViewOfFile → walk IMAGE_NT_HEADERS to locate .text section → memcpy the clean .text over the hooked .text in the loaded ntdll. (3) Per-function stub restore via RtlPcToFileHeader + the on-disk ntdll .text RVA. All three are partial: kernel callbacks (PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutine, ObRegisterCallbacks, CmRegisterCallback) continue to observe operations after userland hooks are removed, so unhooking must be paired with operations that do not trigger callbacks. The fresh-copy variant is operationally preferred because it does not require per-function signature knowledge.
clusters.technical_anchor: MapViewOfFile of fresh \??\C:\Windows\System32\ntdll.dll → IMAGE_NT_HEADERS.OptionalHeader.SizeOfImage → memcpy over hooked ntdll .text
clusters.priority_reason: Three convergence notes identify this as a discrete technique currently buried inside T-016; promoting to its own card surfaces the variant choice.

clusters.canonical_name: Inline Hook Byte-Pattern Forensics and Hot-Patch Prologue
clusters.rationale: Two coverage gaps describe the same EDR inline-hook byte patterns and the 32-bit hot-patch prologue that enables them; both are diagnostics for detecting hooks and unhooking correctly.
clusters.consolidated_description: Documents the exact byte patterns EDRs leave when inline-hooking ntdll, which an operator must recognize before unhooking. 64-bit hooks: 15-byte trampoline `MOV rax, imm64 (48 B8 ...); JMP rax (FF E0)`. 32-bit hooks exploit the `MOV EDI, EDI` hot-patch prologue slot and the five-NOP padding that precedes 32-bit functions — the EDR overwrites the 2-byte hot-patch slot with a 2-byte short jump back into the 5-NOP pad, then patches the pad with a 5-byte `JMP rel32` into the trampoline. The 32-bit pattern is critical because unhooking must restore both the 5-NOP pad and the `MOV EDI, EDI` prologue, not just one. The vault's T-016 ntdll_unhook documentation is implicitly x64-centric; this card adds the 32-bit prologue protocol.
clusters.technical_anchor: 32-bit hot-patch prologue: `MOV EDI, EDI` (8B FF) at function start + 5-NOP pad (90 90 90 90 90) preceding function; 64-bit trampoline bytes `48 B8 <imm64> FF E0`
clusters.priority_reason: Two notes, single operational context (unhooking); merges to round out T-016's x86 coverage.

clusters.canonical_name: x64 ABI, Shadow Space, and Calling Convention for Syscall Stubs
clusters.rationale: Three notes (two coverage gaps, one convergence) all describe the x64 calling convention — RCX/RDX/R8/R9 + stack, 32-byte shadow store at RSP+0..RSP+20h — as the structural constraint on syscall stub construction and ROP frame layout.
clusters.consolidated_description: Reference card documenting the x64 ABI as it constrains syscall stubs and ROP frames. Arguments flow in RCX, RDX, R8, R9, then stack; the caller must reserve a 32-byte shadow store at RSP+0..RSP+20h (eight 8-byte slots) for the callee to spill those four register arguments into. Syscall stubs must respect this even when they merely load the SSN into EAX and execute `syscall` — Ekko (T-005) and direct-syscall stubs from T-002 both rely on the shadow store being writable. ROP frame construction for syscall gadgets must similarly allocate the shadow store before the gadget's epilogue reads back the spilled arguments. Note this is distinct from the hardware Shadow Stack (Intel CET) enforcement.
clusters.technical_anchor: 32-byte shadow store at RSP+0..RSP+20h (8 × 8 bytes); RCX/RDX/R8/R9 first four args, RAX for syscall number
clusters.priority_reason: Three convergence notes; the prerequisite that makes syscall stubs and ROP frames legible across the syscalls category.

clusters.canonical_name: Kernel Call-Stack Origin Check Defeating Direct Syscalls
clusters.rationale: Single convergence note describing a defensive mechanism that breaks direct syscalls and motivates indirect syscalls (T-002); high operational relevance and not currently documented.
clusters.consolidated_description: Documents why direct syscalls (executing `syscall` from implant-owned memory) defeat userland EDR hooks but still fail against kernel-mode components that verify the syscall's return address originates from inside ntdll.dll. EDR kernel drivers (via PsSetLoadImageNotifyRoutine or minifilter altitude registration) walk the call stack at syscall entry using NtQueryInformationThread(ThreadStackLimits) or RtlVirtualUnwind; if the frame immediately below the kernel transition is not within ntdll's image base range, the syscall is flagged. This is the operational reason for indirect syscalls (T-002): jumping into a genuine ntdll `syscall; ret` gadget makes the call stack appear legitimate. Concrete detection primitive: walk the frames, check RSP against the ntdll image range returned by NtQueryInformationProcess(ProcessImageFileName) + RtlImageNtHeader.
clusters.technical_anchor: Kernel call-stack walk via RtlVirtualUnwind at syscall entry; frames outside ntdll.dll image base range (from RtlImageNtHeader on NtQueryInformationProcess(ProcessImageFileName)) are flagged
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but uniquely names the defensive mechanism that motivates the entire indirect-syscall technique; novel relative to T-001..T-074.

clusters.canonical_name: EPROCESS / KPROCESS Object-Manager Visibility Split
clusters.rationale: Single concept note documenting a Windows internals distinction that recurs across T-014/T-015/T-016; prerequisite for understanding handle-vs-kernel-only fields.
clusters.consolidated_description: Documents the kernel object split: EPROCESS is partially exposed via the Object Manager (HandleTable, ImageFileName, UniqueProcessId, Pcb) while _KPROCESS — the embedded head of EPROCESS — holds DirectoryTableBase (CR3 at offset 0x028 on x64), ThreadListHead (offset 0x030), ReadyListHead (offset 0x038), and Affinity (offset 0x040) and is strictly kernel-only. User-mode code cannot read _KPROCESS directly; any technique that requires CR3 pivoting or thread-list walking must obtain a kernel handle or read through NtQuerySystemInformation. This split underpins why T-014 (NtCreateUserProcess) does not expose affinity or page-table root to the caller, and why forensic scanners pivot through EPROCESS→Pcb→ThreadListHead to detect PEB-unlinked modules.

clusters.canonical_name: Thread Hijack Requires CONTEXT Modification

Pairs with T-013's waiting_thread_hijack_ref.rs but elevates the primitive to its own card so the CONTEXT modification step is documented independently.

clusters.canonical_name: Import Address Table (IAT) Hooking Primitive
clusters.rationale: Single coverage-gap note describing the complete 6-step IAT hooking primitive, currently absent from the vault despite being a foundational hooking technique.
clusters.consolidated_description: Documents the IAT hooking primitive in 6 steps: (1) parse the target PE's IMAGE_NT_HEADERS → DataDirectory[IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_IAT (index 12)], or DataDirectory[IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_IMPORT (index 1)] for the descriptor; (2) walk the IMAGE_IMPORT_DESCRIPTOR array (OriginalFirstThunk → INT, FirstThunk → IAT, Name → DLL name); (3) for each imported function, match by name or ordinal; (4) flip the IAT page protection from PAGE_READONLY to PAGE_READWRITE via VirtualProtect (the IAT is typically read-only at runtime); (5) overwrite the function pointer with the hook address; (6) restore PAGE_READONLY. Distinct from inline hooking (which patches function prologue bytes) — IAT hooking only affects calls routed through the IAT, not direct GetProcAddress returns.

clusters.canonical_name: Native Application (NT_main) Execution Surface
clusters.rationale: Two notes (one gap, one emerging-tradecraft) both surface the native Windows application entry signature as a distinct execution mode currently undocumented in the vault.
clusters.consolidated_description: Documents the native Windows application execution mode: entry signature `NTSTATUS NTAPI NT_main(int argc, char* argv[])`, distinct from the Win32 main / WinMainCRTStartup. clusters.canonical_name: IAT and Inline Hooking as EDR Userland Mechanisms
clusters.rationale: Singleton coverage-gap note about the two primary userland hooking mechanisms EDRs employ, which T-016 evades but does not document as background.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 units 35-40 document the two primary userland hooking mechanisms EDRs employ:
IAT pointer overwrite (flipping the IAT entry's memory protection to PAGE_READWRITE via
VirtualProtect, replacing the function pointer with a detour, restoring protection) and
inline prologue patching (overwriting the first 5-7 bytes of the function prologue with
a jmp to the detour, saving the original bytes for pass-through). The vault's T-016
(NTAPI Hook Evasion) evades these hooks by using direct syscalls but does not document
the hook mechanisms themselves as background. A prerequisite card should describe both
hook types, the VirtualProtect-based IAT flip, the inline prologue patch with trampoline
construction, the saved-byte restoration pattern, and how each hook type is detected
(scanning IAT for non-module-range pointers; scanning prologue for jmp opcodes). This
background makes T-016's evasion approach comprehensible to readers without prior EDR
internals knowledge.
clusters.technical_anchor: IAT hook: VirtualProtect PAGE_READWRITE → overwrite function pointer → restore protection; Inline hook: prologue byte patch with jmp rel32 (0xE8/E9) + trampoline with saved original bytes
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents the EDR hook mechanisms that T-016 evades; high prerequisite value for understanding T-016.

classification. The vault's T-021 treats shellcode encoding formats (IPv4/IPv6/MAC/

rationale (presence of a key → encryption; absence of a key → encoding).

clusters.canonical_name: Windows Data Type System as Architecture Portability Rationale
clusters.rationale: Singleton concept note about the Windows data type system (DWORD, BOOL, BOOLEAN) as an architecture-insulation layer; concept node, not a technique.
clusters.consolidated_description:
SEC670 explains that Windows data types (DWORD, BOOL, BOOLEAN, HANDLE, LPVOID) were
created to insulate source code from 16-bit to 32-bit to 64-bit architecture
transitions. BOOL is a 32-bit int (typedef int BOOL), BOOLEAN is a BYTE (typedef
unsigned char BOOLEAN), DWORD is a 32-bit unsigned long (typedef unsigned long DWORD),
and HANDLE is a void* (sizeof varies by architecture). This matters for FFI bindings
(Rust extern "C", Go cgo) where using the wrong native type produces ABI mismatches
that are silent on one architecture but corrupt data on another. A concept card should
document the type hierarchy (Win32 typedefs → C base types → actual sizes by
architecture), the BOOL vs BOOLEAN distinction (4 bytes vs 1 byte — a common source
of FFI bugs), the pointer-size types (HANDLE, LPVOID, PSTR), and how the vault's Rust
bindings map these types (e.g., BOOL → i32, HANDLE → isize, DWORD → u32).
clusters.technical_anchor: BOOL = typedef int (4 bytes, i32 in Rust) vs BOOLEAN = typedef unsigned char (1 byte, u8 in Rust) vs DWORD = typedef unsigned long (4 bytes, u32) vs HANDLE = void* (pointer-sized, isize)
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton concept node; educational completeness value, no direct operational impact.

clusters.canonical_name: Windows Calling Conventions for Syscall Stubs and FFI
clusters.rationale: Singleton concept note about Windows calling conventions (__stdcall, __cdecl, __fastcall, __thiscall) as a prerequisite for syscall stub and FFI implementation.
clusters.consolidated_description:

(Win32 API default, callee cleans stack, arguments pushed right-to-left), __cdecl
(C runtime default, caller cleans stack, variadic-compatible), __fastcall
(first 2 args in ECX/EDX on x86, rest on stack; on x64 superseded by the unified
ABI), __thiscall (C++ member functions, this in ECX on x86). The x64 unified calling
convention (RCX/RDX/R8/R9 for first 4 integer args, XMM0-3 for floats, shadow space
allocation by caller) is the one that actually matters for the vault's syscall stubs
and NT API FFI on x64 Windows. The vault's T-001 through T-006 all assume this
convention but do not document it. A concept card should document each convention's
stack-cleanup responsibility, argument-passing registers, name mangling, and the
x64 unified ABI shadow space (32 bytes) — particularly relevant for hand-rolled
syscall stubs where the shadow space must be allocated or the return address
clobbers the first 8 bytes of where RCX was expected to persist.
clusters.technical_anchor: x64 unified ABI: RCX/RDX/R8/R9 for first 4 integer args, 32-byte shadow space (_RSP+0..0x20) allocated by caller, return value in RAX, stack 16-byte aligned pre-call
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton concept but foundational for understanding all syscall stub implementations (T-001-T-006); high prerequisite value.

resolution for stealthy function lookup. A card should document the .def file syntax,
the linker /DEF flag, the MAKEINTRESOURCE(ordinal) macro for GetProcAddress, the
NONAME/Private attributes, and the detection surface (ordinal-only exports are a known
DLL-cloaking IoC).

clusters.canonical_name: PE Export Directory Traversal for API Resolution
clusters.rationale: Two notes (one convergence, one emerging-tradecraft) both describe the PE export directory traversal as the shared foundation for T-004, T-006, and T-008 — the same mechanism reimplemented as custom GetProcAddress.

e_lfanew → IMAGE_NT_HEADERS → OptionalHeader.DataDirectory[IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_EXPORT]

pointers) → AddressOfNameOrdinals (WORD ordinal array, parallel to names) →
AddressOfFunctions (DWORD RVA array of function pointers, indexed by ordinal). The
resolution algorithm: binary-search AddressOfNames for the target function name, read
the parallel ordinal from AddressOfNameOrdinals, index into AddressOfFunctions with
that ordinal, and add the module base address to get the function's virtual address.

T-004 PEB Walker implements by walking gs:[0x60] → PEB → Ldr → InLoadOrderModuleList

traversal is the shared foundation for T-004 (API resolution), T-006 (module stomping,
which must locate export functions to stomp), and T-008 (thread hijacking, which must
resolve function addresses for hijack targets).

clusters.canonical_name: Handle Leak Discipline After CreateProcess
clusters.rationale: Singleton coverage-gap: PROCESS_INFORMATION returns hProcess and hThread kernel handles that leak in caller's handle table; not documented in injection cards.

leak in the caller's handle table indefinitely. Handle leaks are an
operational opsec hazard: EDR vendors querying

ancestry. The vault's T-013/T-014/T-015 injection cards create processes

document the cleanup discipline. Specific guidance: after NtResumeProcess,
wait for child exit (WaitForSingleObject(hThread, INFINITE)) THEN
CloseHandle(hThread); CloseHandle(hProcess);. Failure to wait before
close leaves zombie threads.

document the suspension mechanics: NtCreateProcessEx returns

with no loaded modules beyond ntdll.dll; LdrpInitialize's APC is queued but
not dispatched until NtResumeProcess triggers KiUserApcDispatcher.

process is in a deterministic uninitialized state ideal for image-base
replacement, PEB unlinking, and module-list hollowing.

clusters.canonical_name: Heaven's Gate (Wow64 32-to-64-bit Syscall Transition)
clusters.rationale: Singleton emerging-tradecraft note: SEC670 documents Heaven's Gate as Wow64-mediated 0x33 segment transition for 32-to-64 syscall dispatch; distinct from T-002 Hell's/Halo's/Tartarus Gate SSN resolution.

32-bit code to 64-bit syscall dispatch via the 0x33 segment selector in the

selectors in TEB fields at offsets 0xC0/0xE0); jumping to a far32 ptr with
selector 0x33 switches CS to the 64-bit segment, allowing execution of
native 64-bit syscall instructions (mov eax, SS; syscall) bypassing the
32-bit Wow64 thunk layer (ntdll!Nt* stub → wow64!Nt* thunk →
wow64cpu!TurboDispatch → 64-bit ntdll). The vault's T-002
(Hell's/Halo's/Tartarus Gate) addresses SSN resolution via unhooked Nt*
stub hashing, which is a different problem (resolving syscall numbers
without Nt* stubs in memory) vs Heaven's Gate (bypassing Wow64 layer for
direct 64-bit syscall dispatch from 32-bit shellcode). The card should
document the 0x33 selector jump pattern, the 0x23 reverse transition, and
modern Win10+ mitigations.

clusters.canonical_name: APC Queue and Thread State Internals
clusters.rationale: Singleton cross-source-convergence note documenting APC queue mechanics and thread Ready/Running/Waiting states as internals prerequisite for injection techniques.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 review material identifies the APC (Asynchronous Procedure Call) queue as the mechanism that lets threads process routines during their quantum, and thread Ready/Running/Waiting states as the scheduling context that determines when an APC is delivered. This is prerequisite internals knowledge for the vault's T-007 Early Bird APC and T-012 thread hijacking techniques — both rely on queuing an APC (NtQueueApcThread) that is delivered when the target enters an alertable state or during thread initialization.

clusters.canonical_name: Suspended Process Creation as Hook-Free Window
clusters.rationale: Singleton emerging-tradecraft note documenting the suspended stage of process creation as the moment free from EDR hooks, explaining why hollowing/early-bird/hijacking work.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 review questions explicitly identify the suspended stage of process creation (between NtCreateProcessEx returning the handle with CREATE_SUSPENDED and the first instruction executing) as the moment free from EDR userland hooks. During this window, the process PEB is initialized, the loader (ntdll!LdrInitializeThunk) has not yet run, and no EDR DLL has been injected via standard AppInit/AppCert/known-dlls mechanisms. The vault's T-012, T-013, and T-016 do not explicitly document this temporal window as the evasion mechanism.
clusters.technical_anchor: CREATE_SUSPENDED flag in NtCreateProcessEx → suspended window before ntdll!LdrInitializeThunk installs EDR hooks
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents the temporal evasion mechanism underlying multiple existing injection techniques

clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents the critical residual detection surface that limits the value of userland unhooking

clusters.canonical_name: Memory Forensics Detection Layer (PE-sieve, Moneta, Volatility)
clusters.rationale: Both notes cross-reference memory scanners as the detection surface that vault injection / evasion cards must address.
clusters.consolidated_description: PE-sieve (Hasherzade), Moneta (forrest-orr), and Volatility (Volatility Foundation) detect in-memory implants even when on-disk AV does not, by scanning process address spaces for unbacked executable regions, hollowed modules, suspicious PE header anomalies, IAT mismatches, and RWX permissions inconsistent with the original image. The vault's detection narrative narrows to kernel callbacks and ETW; the gap leaves operators without a model of how memory scanners fingerprint module stomping (T-007), Threadless injection (T-008), and NTDLL unhooking (T-016). PE-sieve specifically walks the PEB Loader list (PEB->Ldr->InLoadOrderModuleList) and cross-checks each entry against the on-disk image via MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION, flagging modules where ImageBase mismatches or MZ / PE headers indicate shadow copies; Moneta targets unbacked RWX / EXECUTE_READWRITE memory in a more generic fashion.
clusters.technical_anchor: PE-sieve scan: enumerate PEB.Ldr.InLoadOrderModuleList, for each LDR_DATA_TABLE_ENTRY compare MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION.AllocationProtect (PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE vs PAGE_EXECUTE_WRITECOPY) and MappedFileName against ntdll on disk
clusters.priority_reason: Cross-source convergence across SEC670 and Huntress Labs; surfaces detection surface for 6 existing injection / evasion cards

clusters.canonical_name: Kernel-Mode EDR Survives Userland Unhooking
clusters.rationale: Singleton cross-source convergence note that constrains T-016's operational claims about NTDLL unhooking.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 explicitly states that unhooking ntdll does not truly blind a security product because a kernel driver can still observe via PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutine (process create / exit callback), PsSetLoadImageNotifyRoutine (image load callback), PsSetCreateThreadNotifyRoutine (thread create callback), ObRegisterCallbacks (process / thread handle duplication callback), CmRegisterCallback (registry modification callback), and mini-filter FileFilter callbacks. T-016's clean-ntdll-unhook technique therefore only addresses userland-hook-based telemetry; it does not defeat EDRs that operate at the kernel boundary. The vault should make this operational constraint explicit on T-016 so operators understand that unhooking is necessary but not sufficient for evasion against modern EDRs, and that combining T-016 unhooking with callback blocking (kernel-driver-based) is required for full telemetry suppression.
clusters.technical_anchor: PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutine (kernel callback class ProcessCreate / ProcessExit) and PsSetLoadImageNotifyRoutine surviving ntdll userland unhook
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but operational constraint affecting existing T-016 card; high-value correction to vault

clusters.canonical_name: C2 Listener Host Round-Robin Rotation
clusters.rationale: Singleton from CRTO documenting Cobalt Strike listener HA config; fills infrastructure-resilience gap in T-022.
clusters.consolidated_description: CRTO documents Cobalt Strike HTTP listener configuration with round-robin host rotation across multiple HTTP hosts on port 80, providing C2 infrastructure resilience against sinkhole, domain takedown, or single-host seizure. The listener definition accepts a comma-separated Host field and cycles through hosts at the HTTP transport layer, with the teamserver distributing Beacons across the listed hosts during profile generation. The vault's T-022 networking suite does not document this operational pattern for infrastructure redundancy; a card should cover listener HA configuration, the C2-Profile Malleable C2 host rotation syntax, and the operator-side Beacon retry logic that handles per-host failure.
clusters.technical_anchor: Cobalt Strike listener 'Host' field accepting comma-separated HTTP[S] hosts for round-robin rotation on port 80 / 443, plus Malleable C2 profile http-get / http-post uri-append syntax
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton with concrete CRTO tradecraft; infrastructure-resilience gap in T-022

clusters.canonical_name: Reverse Shell Firewall Penetration Tradecraft
clusters.rationale: Singleton foundational note framing reverse-vs-bind shell tradeoffs that inform T-022 design.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 states that reverse shells are mostly preferred over bind shells because they can poke through outbound-permissive firewalls and connect back to the C2 listener. The trade-off: bind shells require inbound port exposure on the target (often blocked by host firewall or egress filtering), while reverse shells originate from inside the network and only need outbound 80 / 443 / 53 (HTTP / HTTPS / DNS). This foundational tradecraft informs the design of T-022's networking stack and the operator's choice between connect-back and bind-listener code paths in an implant; the vault should document the trade-off matrix on T-022 and explicitly call out the Windows Firewall (netsh advfirewall) inbound block behavior that makes reverse shells operationally preferred.
clusters.technical_anchor: Outbound-only TCP connect-back from implant to C2 listener on port 80 / 443 / 53 (HTTP/S/DNS) vs bind-listen on arbitrary port requiring netsh advfirewall firewall add rule inbound ACL
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton with foundational tradecraft; informs T-022 design decisions

clusters.canonical_name: UAC Bypass Discovery Methodology and Tradecraft
clusters.rationale: Three notes converge on UAC bypass methodology + tradecraft across SEC670 modules, UACMe reference, and existing vault cards.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 Lab 3.7 documents a discovery methodology: enumerate System32 binaries, extract PE manifests via mt.exe or by parsing RT_MANIFEST resource (type 24), find autoElevate="true" attribute, run under Process Monitor to capture COM handler loading, find an attacker-controllable handler path via registry hijack, then trigger the autoElevate binary to execute the COM handler at elevated integrity. UACMe (hfire_f0x) provides the canonical reference implementation index numbering 80+ bypasses. The vault's T-021 / T-023 document CMSTP bypass as a finished technique but lack the discovery methodology and the cross-source pattern of: autoElevate manifest + COM InprocServer32 / LocalServer32 registry value pointing to attacker DLL + triggering binary (computerdefaults.exe, sdclt.exe, fodhelper.exe, eventvwr.exe). A consolidated card should document the manifest parsing step (autoElevate attribute location), the COM hijack step (HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID\{<GUID>}\InprocServer32), and the trigger binaries.
clusters.technical_anchor: autoElevate="true" attribute in PE manifest XML (RT_MANIFEST resource type 24) + COM InprocServer32 registry hijack at HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID\{<GUID>}\InprocServer32 triggering via sdclt.exe / fodhelper.exe / computerdefaults.exe
clusters.priority_reason: Three member notes with cross-source convergence; adds methodology depth to existing T-021

clusters.canonical_name: Windows Privilege Escalation Primitives (Admin to SYSTEM)
clusters.rationale: Two notes cross-source converge on the canonical admin-to-SYSTEM escalation privilege set and primitive catalog.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670, MalDev Academy, and CRTO converge on the same five-privilege set as the canonical admin-to-SYSTEM escalation paths: SeTakeOwnership (take ownership of a SYSTEM process binary or service path via SetSecurityInfo, replace with malicious payload, restart service), SeTcbPrivilege (call NtCreateThreadEx inside a SYSTEM process via ZwOpenProcess + thread creation), SeCreateTokenPrivilege (craft a SYSTEM token directly via NtCreateToken specifying SYSTEM SID in TOKEN_USER), SeLoadDriverPrivilege (load unsigned kernel driver via NtLoadDriver that performs PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutineEx manipulation or token theft), SeDebugPrivilege (OpenProcess(PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) on winlogon.exe, DuplicateTokenEx with SecurityImpersonation level, CreateProcessWithTokenW). The vault documents LSASS credential harvest (T-023) and CMSTP UAC bypass (T-021) but has no card cataloging these privilege primitives — they are the building blocks for chaining admin -> SYSTEM -> kernel.
clusters.technical_anchor: SeDebugPrivilege + OpenProcess(PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) on winlogon.exe (PID 508 typical) + DuplicateTokenEx(SecurityImpersonation, TokenPrimary) + CreateProcessWithTokenW for SYSTEM-context execution
clusters.priority_reason: Three-source convergence (SEC670 / MalDev / CRTO) on canonical privilege set; fills a critical prerequisite gap for multiple privesc chains

clusters.canonical_name: GPO Abuse for Domain-Tier Privilege Escalation
clusters.rationale: Singleton emerging-tradecraft note; explicitly flagged as not fitting existing T-NNN scope but worth cataloging for future domain-tier expansion.
clusters.consolidated_description: CRTO covers SharpGPOabuse (Vincent Le Toux) for pushing SYSTEM-context scheduled task execution across GPO-scoped machines by writing malicious ScheduledTasks.xml into the SYSVOL GPO directory on a Domain Controller. The XML takes the form <ScheduledTasks><Task V2="1"><Properties action="Create" name="..." .../> with cdata containing the command, and Group Policy Client (gpsvc.dll, hosted by svchost.exe -k netsvcs) pulls + executes it at next GPO refresh on each scoped host. The technique requires write access to the GPO (typically via Group Policy Creator Privilege delegation or write ACL on the GPO object). The vault's T-NNN scope is Windows-local offensive tradecraft; GPO abuse is domain-tier and currently sits as an orphan cluster without a parent card.
clusters.technical_anchor: SharpGPOabuse writing ScheduledTasks.xml to \\<DC>\SYSVOL\<domain>\Policies\{<GPO-GUID>}\Machine\Preferences\ScheduledTasks\ScheduledTasks.xml with <Task V2="1"> + command cdata
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but represents a distinct tradecraft surface; orphan but cataloged for future scope expansion

clusters.canonical_name: Domain and Active Directory Recon from Standard User Context
clusters.rationale: Two notes address AD / domain recon from non-elevated context — CRTO surface missing from T-023.
clusters.consolidated_description: CRTO documents AD enumeration via PowerView (Get-DomainComputer, Get-DomainUser, Get-DomainGPO, Get-DomainController, Find-DomainUserLocation) and ADSearch with custom LDAP filters — all runnable from standard user context without elevation. Running domain recon from a high-integrity process is operationally detrimental because it conflates the recon footprint with the elevated token (token duplication context, EDR attention). The vault's T-023 covers 'recon' generically but does not document the standard-user AD enumeration layer that bridges initial access and lateral movement; the card should enumerate PowerView cmdlets, ADSearch LDAP filter syntax, and the operational guidance that recon must be performed in the initial standard-user context.
clusters.technical_anchor: PowerView Get-DomainComputer -LDAPFilter '(operatingSystem=*Server*)' invoking System.DirectoryServices.DirectorySearcher against LDAP://CN=Configuration,DC=... rootDSE
clusters.priority_reason: Two member notes with cross-source convergence (CRTO); fills a critical gap between initial access and lateral movement

clusters.canonical_name: Anti-VM Detection Primitive API Catalog

clusters.canonical_name: Host Recon Surface Catalog (Registry, WMI, KUSER, SDDL, sc.exe)
clusters.rationale: Two notes describe the host recon surface catalog and recon API selection consensus across SEC670 / CRTO.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 recon material forms a host recon surface catalog: registry hives (HKU ProfileList for user SID discovery via ProfileImagePath, HKLM SAM for local account hashes, HKLM SECURITY for cached domain creds under HKLM\SECURITY\Cache, HKLM SYSTEM CurrentControlSet for service / driver inventory, HKLM SOFTWARE Microsoft Windows CurrentVersion Uninstall for installed products, HKCU Software for user-installed apps), WMI Win32 provider classes (Win32_Process, Win32_Service, Win32_Registry, Win32_OperatingSystem, Win32_NetworkAdapterConfiguration), KUSER_SHARED_DATA direct read, ProfileList for SID enumeration, sc.exe security descriptors for service ACL mapping via sc.exe sdshow. The API selection consensus: GetAdapterAddresses vs GetNumberOfInterfaces vs GetIpStatistics distinction; CreateToolhelp32Snapshot vs WTSEnumerateProcesses vs WMI Win32_Process for process enumeration; each pair maps to a different signal / detail trade-off.
clusters.technical_anchor: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Disk\Enum key + WMI Win32_NetworkAdapterConfiguration (GetAdaptersAddresses) + HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\<GUID> subkey enumeration
clusters.priority_reason: Two member notes with cross-source consensus; consolidates 6+ recon surfaces into one navigable catalog

clusters.canonical_name: WMI as Dual-Use Recon and Persistence Channel
clusters.rationale: Two notes converge on WMI as a single substrate for both recon (Win32_*) and persistence (__EventFilter / __EventConsumer) — operationally distinct from a single-purpose WMI card.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 Book 4 (Persistence) and Book 2 (Recon) both use WMI — Book 4 for __EventFilter / __EventConsumer / __FilterToConsumerBinding persistence binding in root\subscription namespace, Book 2 for Win32_Process / Win32_Service / Win32_Registry enumeration via Get-WmiObject or IWbemServices::ExecQuery. CRTO also surfaces WMI via Get-Domain / Get-DomainController PowerShell cmdlets. The convergence point: WMI is the single Windows management substrate that supports both recon (read via ExecQuery on standard namespaces root\cimv2, root\default) and persistence (write via permanent event subscription in root\subscription) using the same COM interfaces (CoCreateInstance(CLSID_WbemLocator, IID_IWbemLocator) -> IWbemLocator::ConnectServer -> IWbemServices::ExecQuery / PutInstance). The vault's T-023 recon card and T-017 persistence card both miss the dual-use nature, which means the same COM channel can be used to enumerate the host and to establish persistence in a single IWbemServices session.
clusters.technical_anchor: WMI permanent event subscription: __EventFilter (Query) + __EventConsumer (CommandLineEventConsumer) + __FilterToConsumerBinding in root\subscription namespace, all written via IWbemServices::PutInstance
clusters.priority_reason: Two member notes with cross-source convergence; surfaces WMI dual-use nature absent from both T-017 and T-023

clusters.canonical_name: Registry Hive Operational Map
clusters.rationale: Singleton covering SEC670's 10-unit registry hive enumeration — too foundational to drop or split.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 dedicates 10 units to enumerating the six registry hives with operational implications: HKU\.DEFAULT and HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\ProfileList\<SID> for user SID discovery (ProfileImagePath value), HKLM\SAM for local account hashes (encrypted, requires SYSTEM token to read via RegSaveKeyEx or RegReadValue; typically read offline via secretsdump.py after RegSaveKey), HKLM\SECURITY for cached domain creds (NL$ keys under HKLM\SECURITY\Cache, 16-byte NLKM + cached domain hashes), HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services for driver / service inventory, HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall for installed products (DisplayName, DisplayVersion, UninstallString), HKCU\Software for user-installed apps and config. The vault lacks a navigable operational map tying each hive to specific recon / persistence primitives; a reference card should enumerate the hive paths, the SYSTEM-token requirement, and the typical secrets dump pipeline (reg save -> secretsdump.py -> Mimikatz).
clusters.technical_anchor: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\ProfileList\<SID> ProfileImagePath value + HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$ keys for cached domain credentials
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but operationally foundational; 10 SEC670 units support this single reference card

clusters.canonical_name: NTFS Directory Entry Table Tradecraft Beyond File Walks
clusters.rationale: Singleton emerging-tradecraft note extending beyond documented directory walks into NTFS-specific primitives.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 introduces the NTFS directory entry table ($I30 index) as the storage substrate behind directory walks (FindFirstFile / FindNextFile enumerate $I30 entries) but does not extend into NTFS-specific tradecraft. Adjacent primitives include MFT parsing via FSCTL_GET_NTFS_FILE_RECORD (0x9006B) on a volume handle returning MFT records via DeviceIoControl, USN journal enumeration via FSCTL_READ_USN_DATA (0x9006F) and FSCTL_QUERY_USN_JOURNAL (0x9006C), alternate data stream (ADS) access via the syntax "<filename>:<streamname>:$DATA", and NTFS Extended Attributes via NtQueryEaFile / NtSetEaFile. The vault's T-017 NTFS EA persistence layer only obliquely references the underlying primitives; a card should document the $I30 index attribute type 0x30 (FILE_NAME) and $ATTRIBUTE_LIST_ENTRY structure, plus the MFT record parsing approach for telemetry-light file enumeration.
clusters.technical_anchor: FSCTL_GET_NTFS_FILE_RECORD (0x9006B) on volume handle returning MFT record via DeviceIoControl; $I30 index attribute type 0x30 (FILE_NAME) in MFT record
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but extends existing T-017 NTFS EA layer with concrete primitives; emerging tradecraft
